To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the temperature sum required for flowering of winter wheat cultivar released between 1952 and 2006 declined by 14–18%, and changes in the cultivar properties contributed as much as changes in the mean growing season temperature to the advancement in the flowering date of winter wheat in Germany.
the phenology of modern winter wheat cultivars has changed and that the changes in phenology are due to changes in cultivar properties rather than changes in sowing date.
the effect of climate change on wheat phenology strongly depends on the cultivar change, and that this effect is much stronger than the effect of climate warming.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the phenology of a crop species is determined by the cultivar or the environment in which it is grown.
a better understanding of the effects of climate change and the role of cultivars on crop phenology.
a better understanding of the role of changes in cultivars in crop phenology trends, which is important for the development of more robust climate change impact assessments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the phenology of modern winter wheat cultivars is more sensitive to temperature change than that of the cultivars of the 1950–1960s.
the effect of the change in the cultivar on the flowering day is as strong as the effect of the increase in the temperature.
changes in cultivar properties have a significant impact on the response of crop phenology to climate change.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the effect of climate change on wheat phenology can be different depending on cultivars.
climate change has affected wheat phenology, and that the effects of climate change are more pronounced than the effects of changes of wheat cultivars.
the phenological response of winter wheat to climate warming is strongly dependent on the choice of cultivar.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the phenology of winter wheat is not solely determined by temperature but is also influenced by the properties of the cultivars used.
the effect of climate change on crop phenology depends on the cultivar change, which has been overlooked so far in most of the climate change impact assessments.

the phenological changes of winter wheat cultivar released between 1952 and 2013 are driven by changes in the temperature requirements for the phenological development stages and not by changes in the sowsing date or the cultivar maturity.
